papers.title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
papers.abstract: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

papers.title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
papers.abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

papers.title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
papers.abstract: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

papers.title: Flow Virometry-Based Profiling of Viral Population Diversity
papers.abstract: Viruses exhibit great phenotypic heterogeneity. Flow virometry enables high-throughput analysis of phenotypic diversity in viral populations, while flow-based sorting allows subpopulations to be isolated for separate characterization. Despite their advantages, flow virometry and sorting have not yet been widely adopted in virology partly because of limited protocols and underexplored applications. Here, we provide a practical guide for analyzing and quantifying virus particles from diverse families using flow virometry enhanced by fluorescence labeling. We further explore applications beyond basic and static characterization of virus populations. We demonstrate that flow virometry can report on interactions between virions and binding partners, as well as between virions. It provides a particle denominator that, combined with genome copy measurements, enables estimation of viral population ploidy. We also show how dynamic processes, such as viral membrane fusion, can be measured in real time. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of sorting virions based on their intrinsic properties, such as morphology, for downstream study. This practical guide provides a roadmap for wider implementation of flow virometry in virology, while the applications illustrated here demonstrate potential to address a variety of questions about virion properties, interactions, and dynamics at the single-particle level.

papers.title: Spatial coordination of peptidoglycan synthesis by MreB directs morphogenesis in Xanthomonas citri
papers.abstract: The cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ coordinate cell wall synthesis during elongation and division in rod shaped bacteria. How these two systems interact in the citrus canker pathogen Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri (X. citri) remains unclear. Previously, we showed that disruption of FtsZ ring placement, by deletion of minC, uncouples cell wall synthesis from division, leading to branching and filamentation. Now, using a MreB-GFP sandwich fusion, we show that MreB localizes at the inner membrane, independently of MinC. Peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis (visualized with the fluorescent D-amino acid analogue HADA) happens mostly at the division septum. Perturbation of MreB with A22 disrupts rod shape maintenance and leads to a dose-dependent growth inhibition. A22 induces a reversible relocalization of MreB into the cell cap region, which is accompanied by a shift of PG synthesis from midcell to the poles. This indicates that MreB is required for proper spatial regulation of PG insertion. This loss of spatial control is exacerbated in {Delta}minC cells, which display increased A22 sensitivity, indicating a synthetic dependence on MreB when FtsZ ring placement is affected. Furthermore, MreB inhibition disrupts ParABS-mediated chromosome segregation, leading to anucleate cells. Our findings establish MreB as a key coordinator of cell wall synthesis, cell shape, and chromosome segregation in X. citri

papers.title: Comparative exometabolome and extracellular-vesicle metabolome of Bifidobacterium
papers.abstract: Bifidobacterium species are early colonisers of the human gut and are widely used as probiotics, yet their extracellular chemistry remains largely unexplored, and the small-molecule cargo of their extracellular vesicles (EVs) has not been characterised. We carried out an exploratory, descriptive characterisation of the exometabolome and EV metabolome of Bifidobacterium longum 35624 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis at 24 and 48 h of anaerobic growth, using untargeted LC MS/MS coupled with feature-based molecular networking and semi-targeted analysis of conjugated lipids. The two strains reshaped the shared culture medium through distinct, strain-specific nutrient conversions. B. longum 35624 deamidated nicotinamide to nicotinic acid and produced the tryptophan catabolite indole 3 lactic acid, whereas B. animalis subsp. lactis catabolised purine nucleosides and accumulated hypoxanthine; the two strains also differed in carbohydrate utilisation. EVs, purified by ultracentrifugation and size exclusion chromatography and characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis, immunoassay and electron microscopy, carried a sparse small-molecule cargo. A membrane glycolipid represented the clearest vesicle-associated signal of bacterial origin, whereas bile acid and N acyl lipid conjugates were also detected but could not be attributed to bacterial production, as they were present in the culture medium. Together, these data provide a first reference description of the Bifidobacterium exometabolome and EV metabolome and identify strain specific extracellular metabolic activities as priorities for targeted validation.

papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of human astrovirus VA1-infected intestinal organoids reveals cell-type-specific responses and a requirement for cholesterol biosynthesis during infection
papers.abstract: Human astroviruses are prevalent but understudied enteric viruses that cause gastroenteritis and neurological disease, particularly in children and immunocompromised individuals. No vaccines or antivirals are available, partly because their biology and pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize transcriptional responses to VA1, a non-classical human astrovirus associated with the majority of extraintestinal disease cases, in fetal ileum-derived human intestinal organoids. VA1 altered epithelial cell-type proportions and progressively spread through the organoids. Differential gene expression analysis of enterocytes and progenitor cells, the cells most prevalent in the organoid model, revealed shared antiviral responses, including interferon signaling, as well as cell-type-specific responses. Enterocytes exhibited a broader early transcriptional response and specifically upregulated cholesterol metabolism and biosynthesis pathways at 1 dpi. By 3 dpi, progenitor cell-specific genes suggested inflammatory and epithelial-defense responses. In two different intestinal epithelial cell lines, T84 and Caco-2 cells, limiting extracellular lipid availability did not alter replication but increased VA1 binding in Caco-2 cells. Pharmacologic inhibition of cholesterol biosynthesis and 25-hydroxycholesterol treatment reduced VA1 replication, while disrupting intracellular cholesterol transport had no detectable effect. Together, these findings expand our knowledge on HAstV biology by defining shared and cell-type-specific epithelial responses to VA1 infection and identifying cholesterol biosynthesis as an important host pathway for successful VA1 replication.

papers.title: Exploitative competition among different dormancy strategists shapes community diversity, recovery from perturbations and response to dispersal
papers.abstract: Dormancy is a reversible physiological state of reduced metabolic activity that occurs in plants and animals, but is particularly common among microorganisms. Microorganisms can switch into dormancy spontaneously or in response to environmental cues. While previous work has investigated the ecological and evolutionary consequences of the switching mechanism, it is unknown how different dormancy-switching mechanisms within a microbial community interact to shape composition and community-level response to environmental changes. Here, we used mathematical modelling to investigate how different microbial strategies for entering and existing from dormancy shape community dynamics under stable conditions, following perturbation, and after dispersal. We modelled strategists that had no dormant state (non-switching), those that employed spontaneous switching, those that switched given a cue (triggered switching), and those that used a combination of spontaneous and triggered switching (mixed switching). We also examined how competition and the costs of switching influence activity dynamics within the community. Our simulations revealed the importance of exploitative competition among dormancy strategists in shaping the community response to perturbation and dispersal. In a mixed community containing different dormancy strategists, spontaneous switchers maintained a dormant pool, but suffered an implicit competitive disadvantage. Meanwhile, triggered switchers were more competitive under favourable conditions but could be pushed into dormancy by exploitative competition from other strategists. Interestingly, dispersal events could intensify competition, induce dormancy in resident populations and alter the relative activity of different strategists, while also restoring community members lost during perturbation. To evaluate these predictions, we then analysed an existing dataset of soil mesocosms that experienced heat perturbation and subsequent dispersal. The data showed a stable dormant pool, consistent with the presence of stochastic switchers, and the observed dormancy dynamics following dispersal supported competition-driven inactivation among triggered switching strategists. However, we found no evidence that dormancy provides general protection against the heat perturbation. Instead, the results suggest that survival may depend on the inherent tolerance of community members, while subsequent recovery reflects the interplay between dormancy, immigration, and competition. Our work shows how dormancy not only impacts community-level resilience to perturbations but also alters, and is altered by, exploitative competition among community members.

papers.title: EFFECT OF A LACTOBACILLUS POSTBIOTIC ON DIGESTIVE HEALTH IN DOGS RAISED IN CONDITIONS AT RISK OF GIARDIA DUODENALIS INFECTION
papers.abstract: Giardia duodenalis infection is associated with diarrhea and dysbiosis in dogs, while metronidazole treatment can further disrupt the microbiota. We evaluated adjunctive LB fermentate HF (LBHF), a Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic, in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 30 naturally infected dogs (Terriers). Animals received metronidazole (50 mg/kg/day) with LBHF (50 mg/kg/day) or microcrystalline cellulose placebo (70 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. Clinical outcomes, fecal biomarkers, canine dysbiosis index, and cyst shedding were monitored over 45 days. Fecal shotgun metagenomics was performed at baseline and day 45. After baseline covariate adjustment, LBHF was associated with significantly lower Giardia burdens during treatment, particularly at days 10 and 20, improved fecal consistency, and reduced odor. No significant effects were found for fecal calprotectin, secretory IgA, blood biomarkers of digestive function, or canine dysbiosis index. Overall microbiome turnover was similar between groups, but multivariate analyses identified distinct treatment-associated community trajectories. LBHF was associated with increased Bacteroidota representation and functional capacity for plant polysaccharide degradation, alongside depletion of gene sets involved in flagellar assembly, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and epithelial-cell signaling. Baseline microbiome composition also predicted Giardia burden, highlighting an association between parasite load and bacterial community structure. Adjunctive LBHF supplementation was associated with faster resolution of canine giardiasis, improved fecal quality, and coordinated microbiome remodeling. Further mechanistic studies are needed to establish whether the observed microbiome functional changes contribute to parasite clearance and recovery of intestinal health.

papers.title: Persistence of Non-industrial Gut Microbiota Discriminates Health and Disease States in Industrial Populations
papers.abstract: Industrialization has sharply reduced gut microbial diversity, possibly affecting human health. To isolate the effects of industrialization, we assembled 18,075 human metagenomes spanning hunter-gatherer, agro-pastoral, and industrial lifestyles. We confirmed individual-level diversity reductions in industrial populations, but also found that nearly all known human-associated microbes exhibit population-level persistence. Previously hypothesized 'vanishing' microbes are reduced from high prevalence in non-industrial populations to above-median prevalence in industrial populations. Species-level signatures in industrial case-control cohorts suggest that harboring 'vanishing' taxa can be associated with health or pathology, depending on the condition. Controlling for background prevalence, 'vanishing' microbes were more likely associated with cases than controls in obesity, both 'vanishing' microbes and those now 'blossoming' in industrialized populations were associated with glucose intolerance, while 'blossoming' taxa were associated with inflammatory bowel disease. We conclude that most microbes have not gone extinct under industrialization, and that the health effects of lifestyle-associated taxa are context-dependent.

papers.title: Persistence of commensal Escherichia coli strains and plasmid transfer in a healthy adult
papers.abstract: Little is known about the ecological dynamics of Escherichia coli strains in the healthy human intestinal tract. Here, the composition of commensal E. coli in a healthy adult was tracked over 700 days. 100 E. coli isolates recovered directly from each of 21 faecal samples collected at monthly intervals were characterised. In total 15 strains were recovered; five were resistant to one or more antibiotics. Five "persistent" strains were found in multiple samples spanning 1- to 5-month periods. The relative abundance of persistent strains ranged from 1-100% of E. coli per sample, but they were dominant (>80%) in 14/21 samples and the only strain in 12. Complete genomes were determined for all strains, including isolates of persistent strains from their first and last appearances. Persistent strains belonged to phylogroups B2 (ST1236 and ST420), A (ST10 and ST93), or D (ST362). Single-sample strains were phylogroup A, B1, B2, D or F. Confirming extended survival in the gut, only minor changes were detected in the chromosomes of persistent strains over their residence periods. However, one lost a plasmid and two gained plasmids, providing evidence for horizontal gene transfer in the gut. A Z-type multidrug resistance plasmid moved from one persistent strain to the next and exchanged a small backbone region with a plasmid in the recipient. An M-type arsenic resistance plasmid was acquired by two different strains and transferred to laboratory E. coli with two co-resident plasmids. All persistent strains, but only 2/10 single-sample strains, carried one or more plasmid-borne bacteriocin determinants.

papers.title: History of coadaptation to the cag pathogenicity island in Helicobacter pylori
papers.abstract: Most Helicobacter pylori strains use genes encoded on the cag pathogenicity island (cagPAI) to inject the CagA oncoprotein into human cells, where it alters cell signalling and morphology to promote bacterial colonization. However, cag- H. pylori strains are found worldwide. Here, we use a global sample of >9,000 Helicobacter genomes to investigate how strains adapt to cag status. We identified variants genome-wide associated with cagPAI presence, including many in vacA and hopQ, as well as in genes not previously linked to cag. We use these variants to construct a cag polygenic coadaptation score, allowing us to systematically explore the dynamics and evolutionary history of the island. Score distribution is bimodal in many populations, showing there is a stable adaptive strategy associated with cag- status. However, these cag- coadapted variants have historically been unavailable to strains in East Asia, providing a potential explanation for the low frequency of cag- strains in this region. We also infer that the cagPAI arrived in H. pylori before the human populations which colonized Australia and Papua New Guinea split from other groups 50,000-70,000 years ago. Adaptation to the island in other populations was achieved in part by using existing variants from the Hardy ecospecies. Our study illustrates how gene coadaptation shapes pathogen evolution after import of a major virulence factor and highlights genetic configurations that may predict increased or decreased disease risk, informing eradication strategies.

papers.title: BRO is a proteinaceous binding receptor for human coronavirus OC43
papers.abstract: Embecoviruses such as human coronavirus (HCoV) OC43 have long been viewed as sialic acid-dependent viruses that attach to cells through interactions with cell surface sialoglycans. Here, we identify a specific proteinaceous receptor that harbors the sialoglycan determinant and also contributes protein contacts for viral spike (S) recognition. Using an unbiased surfaceome CRISPR activation screen for OC43 spike binding, we discovered that the previously uncharacterized human gene C1ORF54 encodes this receptor, which we name Binding Receptor for OC43 (BRO). BRO engages the OC43 S N-terminal domain through O-linked 9-O-acetylated sialoside determinants and neighboring protein contacts. BRO expression in human cells promotes OC43 infection, whereas BRO knockout or blockade with the BRO ectodomain or anti-BRO antibody inhibit infection, including in differentiated primary human airway cultures. BRO orthologs from diverse mammals support OC43 infection when expressed in human cells, suggesting potential contributions to OC43 zoonotic circulation and cross-species transmission. Our findings reshape our understanding of OC43 entry, and pave the way to develop countermeasures targeting this receptor interaction.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal a cyst-neuron-microglia network underlying brain damage during Toxoplasma gondii infection
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii infects approximately one-third of the world's population, and persistent brain infection links to neuropsychiatric disorders. How cysts interact with host brain cells and tissue to sustain infection and cause neuronal damage remains unclear. We combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing with Stereo-seq spatial transcriptomics to map mouse brains across acute and chronic T. gondii infection. We found neurons in the cyst neighbourhood recruit interferon-responsive microglia via the APP-CD74 axis; these microglia breached the cyst wall with invasive pseudopodia, the released parasites formed secondary cysts; and microglial depletion with PLX5622 during chronic infection significantly reduced brain cyst burden, supporting that continual cyst turnover facilitates persistent infection. In mice with chronic infection, suppressed NMDA receptor signalling, enhanced complement-mediated synaptic pruning, impaired adult neurogenesis, and induced lipid reprogramming was found in the cyst neighbourhood. This cyst-neuron-microglia network thus underpins both infection persistence and neuronal injury, offering new mechanistic insights into pathogen-host interactions.

papers.title: Gram-positive bacteria have different susceptibilities to the host-derived antimicrobial lysophosphatidylcholine and adapt to lysophosphatidylcholine-induced stress via distinct mechanisms
papers.abstract: The human lipid metabolites, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and plasmenyl-LPC (pLPC), modulate both the metabolic health status and innate immunity of an individual. Previous studies reported direct antibacterial activity of LPC, while pLPC has not been evaluated. Meanwhile, some bacteria harvest LPC for producing phosphatidylcholine (PC); others produce plasmalogens under anaerobic conditions. These discoveries suggest that both LPC and pLPC can mediate host-microbe interactions. In this study, we demonstrated diverse susceptibility profiles of human pathobionts to LPC(18:0) and pLPC(18:0) at physiologically-relevant concentrations. Though the Gram-negative bacteria Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were not susceptible to LPC or pLPC, all tested Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus agalactiae, Enterococcus faecalis, and E. faecium were susceptible to pLPC, suggesting robust antimicrobial activity of this lipid in vivo. While LPC can effectively kill S. aureus and S. agalactiae, it does not completely inhibit the growth of enterococci. Moreover, pretreatment of LPC-containing medium with E. faecalis rescues S. agalactiae from LPC killing, suggesting that E. faecalis deactivates LPC extracellularly and can protect co-resident LPC-sensitive pathobionts. Finally, we observed the emergence of spontaneous LPC-resistant S. aureus. These strains have point mutations in sensor kinase gene walK and the lipid metabolism genes fabF and farR, which lead to increased expression of the efflux pump gene farE. Collectively, these results support the antibacterial effects of LPC and pLPC and indicate distinct bacterial adaptation mechanisms, providing novel insights on lipid-mediated host-bacterial interactions.

papers.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

papers.title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

papers.title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
papers.abstract: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

papers.title: Pioneering Hybrid Genome Assemblies of Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium avenaceum from Indian Wheat: Insights into Virulence Frameworks and Genome Evolution
papers.abstract: Fusarium head blight (FHB), primarily caused by various species of Fusarium, is a destructive disease of wheat that reduces yield and contaminates grain with mycotoxins. The present study reports high-quality hybrid genome assemblies for two Indian wheat isolates, Fusarium graminearum strain TNW1 and Fusarium avenaceum strain DMW8, representing the first genome-scale comparative study of FHB associated Fusarium isolates infectious on wheat from India. Both Indian isolates retained conserved Fusarium secondary metabolite clusters, including aurofusarin, chrysogine, clavaric acid, koraiol, orcinol/orsellinic acid, and oxyjavanicin, while exhibiting distinct species-associated biosynthetic profiles. TNW1 contained zearalenone and DON-related biosynthetic clusters, whereas DMW8 contained beauvericin and other species -associated clusters, highlighting differences in predicted biosynthetic potential between the two Fusarium species. Notably, both genomes showed relatively low transposable-element (TE) content compared with their respective species groups, with TEs occupying 0.96% of the TNW1 genome and 1.55% of the DMW8 genome. RIP-associated genomic coverage was also comparatively low, at 20.01% and 22.38%, respectively. TE insertion analysis identified predominantly reference-associated insertions, with two candidate non-reference insertions detected in DMW8. Gene-family analyses revealed greater duplication and expansion contraction dynamics in DMW8 than in TNW1. Together, these findings highlight differences in predicted genomic features, secondary metabolite biosynthetic potential, and gene family composition between the two Indian isolates, providing genomic resources for future investigations of Fusarium biology and wheat pathogen interactions.

papers.title: How good a predictor the in vitro antibiogram is, of in vivo antibiotic efficacy? An in vitro - in vivo integrated approach
papers.abstract: Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing, particularly the disc diffusion assay (DDA), provides a convenient means of assessing bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics. However, its ability to predict antibiotic efficacy in an infected host remains uncertain. This study investigated the relationship between DDA-derived inhibition zones and host-protective antibiotic activity using Caenorhabditis elegans infection models involving three bacterial pathogens: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Clostridioides difficile. A total of 42 antibiotics were evaluated through DDA, while a separate panel of 75 antibiotics was screened using an automated C. elegans infection assay. Twenty-six antibiotics common to both panels were selected for comparative analysis. Gnotobiotic L3-L4 stage worms were challenged with individual pathogens in the presence of each antibiotic at a fixed concentration of 9.6 microgram/mL. Worm activity was quantified at 24, 48, and 72 h using an automated worm tracker system, with appropriate health, infection, vehicle, and antibiotic-toxicity controls. Overall, DDA-derived zone of inhibition (ZOI) diameters showed weak-to-moderate, pathogen- and time-dependent correlations with worm activity. At 24 h, Pearson's correlation coefficients ranged from -0.20 to 0.31 across the three pathogen-host systems, while at 48 h they ranged from -0.009 to 0.49. Notably, antibiotic rankings based on DDA and host-protective activity differed considerably. For example, against C. difficile, imipenem produced the largest inhibition zone (41 mm) but failed to protect worms at 24 and 48 h, whereas tobramycin, despite producing a smaller inhibition zone (26 mm), exhibited the highest early worm activity. Similar discrepancies were observed with the other pathogens. These findings demonstrate that DDA-derived susceptibility profiles do not consistently predict antibiotic-mediated protection in an infected host. The C. elegans model may therefore serve as a complementary whole-organism screening platform, providing additional functional information for prioritizing antimicrobial agents beyond conventional in vitro susceptibility testing.

papers.title: Intracellular spirochete integrates into a chemosynthetic micro-consortium of a deep-sea vent mussel
papers.abstract: Animal-microbe interactions comprise a diverse functional landscape, spanning pathogenic to mutualistic outcomes across extracellular and intracellular niches. Within this context, spirochetes are predominantly documented as extracellular associates or transient pathogens, leaving stable, functional endosymbiosis within animal cells unverified. Here, we report the discovery of an intracellular consortium comprising a spirochete and a primary sulfur-oxidizing bacterium within gill bacteriocytes of the deep-sea hydrothermal vent mussel Gigantidas horikoshii. Combining three-dimensional ultrastructural imaging, spatial histology, and multi-omics analyses, we characterize the intracellular spatial architecture and metabolic integration of this system. Both bacteria co-reside within a closed, membrane-bound network of interconnected chambers, where the spirochete is distributed across compartments and occasionally extends across host cell boundaries. Multi-omics profiling uncovers metabolic cooperation between the two bacteria: while the sulfur-oxidizing bacterium provides autotrophic primary production, the spirochete actively transcribes pathways for reactive oxygen species scavenging and organic acid assimilation, likely mitigating localized oxidative stress and acidosis. Coupled with its motility machinery and an expanded repertoire of host-interaction factors, these physiological traits suggest that the spirochete acts as an active stabilizer of the shared intracellular microenvironment. Together, these findings reveal that spirochetes can establish a stable, functional micro-consortium with chemosynthetic bacteria within animal cells, refining the recognized landscape of animal-microbe interactions and illuminating mechanisms linking mutualistic endosymbiosis and intracellular infections.

papers.title: Effect of neuB deletion on biofilm formation and extracellular electron transfer in Geobacter sulfurreducens
papers.abstract: The extracellular matrix of Geobacter sulfurreducens biofilms is primarily composed of proteins and exopolysaccharides. The extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix provides the structural scaffold necessary to facilitate extracellular electron transfer (EET); however, the specific role of its carbohydrate components remains unexplored. Sialic acids are a class of carbohydrate derivates that can modulate extracellular matrix stability in bacteria. N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac), the most common sialic acid, is primarily synthesized by NeuB. We hypothesized that the neuB gene homolog in G. sulfurreducens (gsu1970), putatively involved in Neu5Ac synthesis, plays a key role in EPS organization and EET performance. Deletion of neuB reduced insoluble Fe(III) oxide reduction by approximately 91%. Furthermore, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) revealed that the {Delta}neuB strain formed significantly less dense EPS matrices on both hematite and fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) electrodes. Interestingly, bioelectrochemical analysis of FTO anodes showed that the mutant produced a 3-fold higher current density and exhibited a more negative open-circuit potential than the wild-type strain. It is important to mention that this enhanced performance on FTO is linked to a significant upregulation of omcS, however, more specific experiments need to be performed to establish a definitive causal relationship between omcS transcription levels and the observed bioelectrochemical enhancement. This transcriptional change was not observed during growth on hematite. Our results suggest that neuB expression contributes to maintaining the structural integrity of the WGA-reactive glycoconjugates within the EPS matrix during insoluble iron reduction. Conversely, its absence is associated with a compensatory upregulation of omcS on FTO electrodes. Overall, this study highlights the potential importance of putative sialic acids-related biosynthetic pathways in Desulfuromonadia, showing that alteration of EPS carbohydrate biosynthetic genes can markedly influence both iron reduction and the performance of electroactive biofilms behavior.

papers.title: A metacommunity of complex microbial communities shows high spatial synchrony, ecological memory, gradual succession and invasion resistance
papers.abstract: Complex microbial communities are increasingly applied in biotechnological and health-related environments, yet maintaining their diversity and relative community composition over extended periods remains challenging. While dispersal can counteract the divergence of spatially separated communities, it remains unclear whether controlled mass transfer can sustain compositional synchrony in highly diverse communities over extended periods, whether this synchrony persist after dispersal is interrupted, and how robust such communities are to invasion. Here, we investigate these questions using a loop-design reactor (LDR) comprising five local wastewater microbial communities connected by controlled mass transfer. The experiment covered multiple rounds of alternating mass transfer and insular phases over a time frame of 318 days, different mass transfer intensities, and the introduction of defined microbial invaders. Community dynamics were monitored at a high temporal resolution by single-cell flow cytometry and complemented by metagenomic analyses of selected samples to characterize taxonomic compositions and functional potential. A Bray-Curtis-based Synchrony Index revealed that controlled mass transfer established high compositional synchrony among five local communities, which persisted for more than 150 generations. Although the community structures underwent gradual succession, the local communities remained synchronized, demonstrating parallel rather than divergent temporal trajectories. Interruption of dispersal initially promote divergence, whereas during later insular phases high compositional similarity persisted in the absence of mass transfer, consistent with ecological memory. Introduced microbial species failed to establish within resident communities, indicating high invasion resistance. Community functional potential remained largely stable throughout the experiment, although phosphorus accumulation failed during phases of high mass transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled mass transfer can maintain long-term spatial synchrony of complex microbial communities while allowing gradual community succession. Repeated connectivity promoted compositional similarity beyond periods of active dispersal while maintaining invasion resistance and functional stability, highlighting controlled dispersal as a promising community-level strategy for managing complex microbial communities.

papers.title: LuxS Inactivation Increases Antibiotic Susceptibility and Impairs Genetic Competence in Streptococcus pneumoniae
papers.abstract: The LuxS enzyme participates in bacterial metabolism and produces the precursor of autoinducer-2 (AI-2), a signaling molecule implicated in bacterial stress responses and genetic competence. Although LuxS/AI-2 has been associated with antibiotic responses in other streptococci, its contribution to antibiotic susceptibility in Streptococcus pneumoniae remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of LuxS in pneumococcal survival during exposure to erythromycin and ampicillin and examined whether supplementation with 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD), the precursor of AI-2, could alleviate the effects of luxS inactivation. The {Delta}luxS mutant exhibited significantly greater reductions in viable cell counts than the wild type following antibiotic exposure, even after accounting for differences in baseline growth. Supplementation with 50 nM DPD significantly improved mutant survival during exposure to both antibiotics. We further investigated the contribution of LuxS/AI-2 to genetic competence, a phenotype previously associated with luxS inactivation. The mutant exhibited reduced transformation efficiency, which was significantly improved by DPD supplementation, although recovery remained partial. Together, these findings provide evidence that LuxS contributes to pneumococcal survival during antibiotic exposure and demonstrate that exogenous DPD can partially compensate for the effects of luxS inactivation on antibiotic responses and genetic transformation. These results extend our understanding of LuxS/AI-2-associated phenotypes in S. pneumoniae.

papers.title: Reconstitution in JCVI-syn3B suggests the roles of the Spiroplasma Fibril protein (Sfibril) in swimming
papers.abstract: Spiroplasma, wall-less helical bacteria of the class Mollicutes, swim without flagella by shifting the handedness of their helical body. This motility is driven by an internal ribbon composed of actin-superfamily MreB proteins (SMreB) and the Spiroplasma-specific Fibril protein (Sfibril), which accounts for nearly half of the ribbon mass. However, because helical shape and swimming have been reconstituted with SMreBs alone, the role of Sfibril has remained unclear. Here, we expressed Fibril from Spiroplasma eriocheiris under its native promoter in the minimal synthetic bacterium JCVI-syn3B (syn3), in which swimming had been reconstituted with SMreB proteins, and analyzed cell morphology and swimming. Sfibril formed filaments with chained ring units in syn3 cells and, by itself, induced cell elongation and left-handed helical shape. Elongated cells expressing Sfibril recovered their length after hypo-osmotic shock, indicating that Sfibril confers morphological robustness. In cells expressing SMreB4 and SMreB5 from Spiroplasma, Sfibril increased the fraction of helical and motile cells, extended the distance of continuous kink propagation, reduced cell bending, and increased traveling distance. In addition, Sfibril altered the handedness of SMreB5-driven helices from exclusively right-handed to a mixture of right- and left-handed. These results suggest that Sfibril is not essential for helicity shift but stabilizes the cell body and supports efficient, processive helicity shifts.

papers.title: Charting the Expansive Outer Membrane β-Barrel Landscape in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Outer-membrane beta-barrel (OMBB) proteins are central to Gram-negative bacterial physiology, mediating nutrient acquisition and secretion while shaping host interactions and antimicrobial permeability. Yet tools to catalog the diversity and functional potential of the OMBB proteome in these bacteria remain incompletely defined. Here, we combine proteome-scale structure prediction analysis and experimental validation to systematically map the OMBB proteome of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We identify 105 proteins containing predicted OMBB domains with 8-26 beta-strands, substantially expanding the repertoire across major structural classes and revealing previously unrecognised domain architectures. Comparison with experimentally defined structures shows that prediction accurately captures global barrel architecture but systematically overestimates beta-strand continuity and underrepresents flexible extracellular loops, key determinants of molecular recognition. We then defined the cryo-EM structures of PA2590 and PA3535 (EprS), confirming their predicted functions as a TonB-dependent transporter and an autotransporter, respectively. Using structural prediction, we also identified the phospholipase A1-like activity in the uncharacterized autotransporter PA4579, linking a predicted catalytic site to function. Together, our findings expand the structural and functional landscape of the P. aeruginosa OMBB proteome and establish a generalizable framework for converting proteome-scale structural predictions into experimentally testable mechanisms, enabling discovery of functions hidden within poorly annotated outer-membrane proteomes.

papers.title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
papers.abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

papers.title: Compartment-associated filtering and environmental gradients shape fungal communities in arid Artemisia species
papers.abstract: Plant-associated fungal communities are shaped by interactions among host, environmental conditions, and compartment-specific filtering processes, yet the relative importance of these drivers remains poorly understood in arid and semi-arid ecosystems. We investigated fungal communities associated with three Artemisia species (Artemisia herba-alba Asso., Artemisia mesatlantica Maire and Artemisia negrei L.), including Moroccan endemics, across bulk soil, rhizosphere, root, and shoot compartments using ITS amplicon sequencing, culture-dependent isolation, and ecological analyses. Fungal community composition differed significantly among compartments (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.08, P = 0.012), whereas alpha diversity showed limited variation. Taxonomic profiles revealed compartment-associated shifts, with recurrent fungal genera concentrated in belowground compartments and a higher proportion of unclassified taxa in shoots. Core microbiome analyses identified overlapping fungal taxa between rhizosphere and root communities. Soil physicochemical gradients were associated with fungal community composition, and structural equation modeling indicated significant associations with both environmental variables and plant compartments. Source-tracking analysis attributed approximately 99.4% of root community composition to rhizosphere sources, whereas shoot communities showed contributions from both roots (60%) and the rhizosphere (39%). Culture-dependent isolation recovered 21 fungal isolates, with five genera shared between cultivation and sequencing datasets. Together, these findings reveal compartment-associated fungal community restructuring along the soil?plant continuum and highlight the complementary contributions of environmental conditions, plant-associated habitats, and cultivation-based characterization to understanding fungal microbiomes in arid ecosystems.

papers.title: Host HSP90 mimicry by a parasite effector triggers mitochondrial membrane shedding
papers.abstract: The outer mitochondrial membrane mediates critical host defenses against intracellular pathogens. How microbes manipulate this compartment remains poorly understood. Here, we found that the human parasite Toxoplasma gondii remodels host mitochondrial membranes through molecular mimicry of HSP90 chaperones. Cryo-electron microscopy analyses showed that the parasite effector TgMAF1 binds the same specialized clamp domain of the mitochondrial import receptor TOM70 as chaperones of the HSP70/90 family. Biochemical and comparative genomics analyses demonstrate that this mimicry arose through the neofunctionalization of the TgMAF1 C-terminus from an ancestral paralog incapable of TOM70 binding. In molecular dynamics simulations, complexed TgMAF1-TOM70 triggered the formation of higher order assemblies that induced local membrane curvature. These findings uncover a previously unknown host subversion strategy and establish molecular mimicry of a chaperone as a mechanism for pathogen-driven remodeling of the host OMM.

papers.title: Tissue-specific genomic and transcriptomic dynamics of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in the Pacific oyster Magallana gigas revealed by long-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Ostreid herpesvirus 1 (OsHV-1) causes recurrent mass mortality of juvenile Pacific oysters (Magallana gigas) worldwide, yet its lytic cycle remains poorly characterized in vivo. In the absence of a permissive cell line, most studies have relied on intramuscular injection, which bypasses the natural route of infection, or on primary haemocyte cultures, which cannot capture tissue-level host-virus interactions. In addition, gene expression studies have relied on short-read sequencing, which fragments transcription units and cannot resolve complex transcriptional architectures. Long-read sequencing has recently revealed abundant overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts in other herpesviruses, but whether OsHV-1 shares this complexity, and how its transcriptional program varies across host tissues during natural infection, remains unknown. Here, we exposed naive oysters to OsHV-1 by bath exposure and combined long-read genomic and transcriptomic sequencing of gills, mantle, digestive gland and adductor muscle at increasing levels of infection. OsHV-1 genomes were assembled directly from infected tissues, and intra-host viral diversity was structured by host rather than tissue. We identified 410 unspliced viral transcripts, including overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts. The viral transcriptional program was largely conserved across tissues and resembled that previously described in haemocytes in vitro. In the host, infection triggered a response shared by all tissues, but earlier and stronger in the gills and mantle. Together, these results provide the first long-read view of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in its natural host.
